Dan Ives: AI spending is now starting to translate into revenue Dan Ives, partner at Wedbush Securities, said in an interview with CNBC that the heavy infrastructure investments made by hyperscalers and companies such as Microsoft and NVIDIA are gradually beginning to translate into revenue growth. He said this development is somewhat easing investor concerns about whether massive capital expenditures will ultimately generate sufficient returns. According to Ives, demand remains “uniquely strong.” Once companies build and operate AI systems, they are beginning to commercialize use cases. The enterprise adoption cycle is still in its early stages. Ives argued that fears of a broad collapse in the software sector are exaggerated, saying, “I don’t see a software apocalypse.” He said weakness in names such as ServiceNow is more related to valuation and concentration rather than a fundamental deterioration in the sector. Over the next 6–18 months, he expects use cases in enterprise software, cybersecurity, and companies such as Palantir to become clearer. Overall, Ives estimates that the industry has only gone through roughly 10–15% of the AI revolution. He also noted that investment is expanding into energy and industrial infrastructure. He added that China remains important and that Apple is strengthening its strategy through Alibaba’s technology. The key issue for investors: whether capital expenditures can generate sustainable revenue growth. Ives describes the process as an “arms race.” Source: Dan Ives, CNBC — August 14, 2026. $NVDA $MSFT $AMZN $TSLA $AAPL $META

Wall Street analysts’ classic pro-cyclical behavior in DRAM/NAND stocks (MU, SNDK, SK Hynix, etc.) The memory sector, particularly DRAM and NAND manufacturers such as Micron (MU), SanDisk (SNDK), SK Hynix and Samsung, is one of the clearest examples of Wall Street’s pro-cyclical behavior. When prices rise, price targets are quickly revised upward and “Buy/Overweight” ratings increase. When prices fall, more cautious or bearish notes emerge. This pattern has been especially visible during the 2025–2026 AI-driven memory supercycle. Why does this pattern repeat? 1. Lagging reaction and momentum chasing Sell-side analysts update models using company management, supply-chain checks and hyperscaler feedback. By the time these signals appear in analyst notes, the stock price has often already moved. Targets are therefore frequently raised after much of the rally has occurred. When prices fall, analysts shift toward “peak cycle risk,” “margin pressure” and “capacity expansion.” 2. Herd mentality and career incentives Being far below consensus can create career risk. During rallies, high price targets bring recognition; during downturns, cautious language allows analysts to claim they warned investors early. The memory industry’s history of violent boom-bust cycles, such as 2018 and 2022, reinforces this behavior. 3. Changing valuation frameworks During upcycles, the narrative shifts toward “structural change,” long-term agreements and AI demand, making higher multiples easier to justify. During downturns, the same companies are treated as traditional cyclicals and peak-earnings assumptions are reduced. Examples from 2025–2026 During the rally, Morgan Stanley’s Joseph Moore raised his SNDK target from $1,100 to $1,750 and MU from $520 to $1,050. Cantor Fitzgerald’s CJ Muse raised SNDK to $2,900 and MU to $1,500. BofA, Mizuho, Susquehanna and others followed with aggressive increases. JPMorgan’s August 14, 2026 decision to resume SNDK coverage with an Overweight rating and a $2,250 target continued the trend. Analysts highlighted arguments such as a potentially $500 billion NAND market by 2027, structurally higher margins and multi-year contracts supporting a longer cycle. During the June–August 2026 pullbacks, as some stocks fell 20–50% from their highs, the narrative shifted toward “peak pricing,” future capacity increases and hyperscaler capex risks. More cautious ratings appeared and some targets were lowered. Weaker-than-expected pricing from SK Hynix and Samsung also triggered concerns that the cycle could be nearing a peak. This behavior is frequently criticized on X, where traders argue that price targets often follow the stock price rather than predict it. Comments such as “PT upgrades… now going to get rolled back like clockwork” capture the frustration. Others argue that cautious analyst language can create contrarian buying opportunities. Historical context Similar patterns appeared during the 2017–2018 and 2021–2022 memory cycles: targets were raised near the top, while bearish commentary increased after the decline had already begun. Memory stocks often peak before earnings, while analysts remain tied to backward-looking data. Investor takeaway Analyst targets should be treated as data points, not real-time forecasts. Investors should independently monitor supply, LTA coverage, HBM/NAND bit growth, pricing and hyperscaler capex. For long-term investors, falling prices combined with increasingly bearish commentary can offer better entry points if the structural AI-demand thesis remains intact. For short-term traders, analyst upgrades arriving after major price increases should be treated with caution. Ultimately, $MU , $SNDK and SK Hynix illustrate a classic Wall Street weakness: analysts often follow the cycle rather than anticipate it.

JPMorgan has resumed coverage of SanDisk $SNDK with an Overweight rating and a $2,250 price target. Analyst Harlan Sur views SanDisk as one of the clearest beneficiaries of AI inference fundamentally reshaping NAND demand. The company has already locked in approximately $94 billion in long-term contracts. Even at the lowest pricing levels, these agreements can generate gross margins of around 80%, giving the business model significantly more predictable economics. JPMorgan forecasts the NAND market could surge to $500 billion by 2027. Combined with technological leadership and aggressive share buybacks, this creates a multi-year, compounding earnings growth story.

Stifel upgraded Intuitive Machines $LUNR from Hold to Buy, with a $26 price target. Q2 revenue came in at $206 million, up 310% year over year, but slightly below expectations. Adjusted EBITDA showed a $13.8 million loss, primarily due to an estimate adjustment related to the IM-4 lander. The company reaffirmed its 2026 guidance of $900 million–$1 billion in revenue and positive EBITDA. The real standout was the backlog: it increased from $1.06 billion to $1.76 billion, a $707 million increase. That translates to a 4.5x book-to-bill ratio. Most of the increase came from more than $600 million in commercial GEO satellite orders, with the portfolio spanning civil, commercial, and national security markets. Analyst Jonathan Siegmann upgraded the stock to Buy, citing strong backlog momentum and an attractive valuation following the recent share-price decline. Stifel raised its revenue estimates but lowered the price target to $26 due to capital structure considerations and peer multiples. Source: Stifel note
